lessons.title: Meet your guitar
lessons.summary: Find your way around the instrument.
lessons.see: Rest the guitar securely and let your shoulders relax. The thinnest string is 1; the thickest is 6. A fret number names the space just before that metal fret. Touch a string on the diagram to explore it.
lessons.detail: Your fretting fingers are index 1, middle 2, ring 3, and little finger 4. Press just behind the fret, not on its wire, using only enough pressure for a clear note. Pick one string gently. Pause if anything hurts.
lessons.practice: Play each reference tone and match your open string by ear, or use your own tuner. These are reference pitches, not automatic tuning measurements. Spend a minute finding strings 1 and 6 without rushing.
lessons.recap: You can name the strings, find a fret, and identify your fretting fingers.

lessons.title: Six open strings
lessons.summary: Hear the low-to-high string order.
lessons.see: An open string rings without a fretting finger. Read the board from string 6 to string 1: E, A, D, G, B, E. The two E strings share a letter but sound two octaves apart.
lessons.detail: The hollow circle means open: no fretting finger. The staff uses guitar treble notation, written one octave above what you hear. A sounding high-string E4 is written as E5; the tab and fretboard still mean the open first string.
lessons.practice: Play each open string slowly. Say its name before picking. Then try returning from high E to low E. Repeat twice, leaving time to move your picking hand.
lessons.recap: You have connected six open-string sounds to names and locations.

lessons.title: Your first three notes
lessons.summary: E, F, and G on string 1.
lessons.see: Keep your hand near the nut. Play E open, F with finger 1 at fret 1, and G with finger 3 at fret 3. This is first position: your fingers work near frets 1–4.
lessons.detail: The number inside a lit marker is your finger, not the fret number. Read the fret along the bottom edge. Keep unused fingers relaxed and close to the string.
lessons.practice: Step through E, F, G, F. Say each name and place your finger before picking. Repeat the phrase three times, then try finding F with the labels as your guide.
lessons.recap: You can play E–F–G without moving your hand out of first position.

lessons.title: A second string
lessons.summary: B, C, and D; then cross to string 1.
lessons.see: String 2 gives you B open, C at fret 1 with finger 1, and D at fret 3 with finger 3. Check the string number before placing the finger.
lessons.detail: When crossing strings, move the picking hand only as far as needed. The next-note marker shows where to prepare. Listen for one clear note at a time.
lessons.practice: Play B–C–D, then cross to the open E on string 1. Try the return journey slowly. If a string buzzes, reset your fingertip just behind the fret.
lessons.recap: You can connect two strings into a short musical phrase.

lessons.title: Into the middle
lessons.summary: G–A and D–E–F on strings 3 and 4.
lessons.see: On string 3, play G open and A at fret 2 with finger 2. On string 4, play D open, E at fret 2 with finger 2, and F at fret 3 with finger 3.
lessons.detail: Some note letters appear in several octaves. Use the staff height and string number together. These middle-string notes sound lower than the notes from your first two strings.
lessons.practice: Explore each string separately, then join the phrase. Keep the wrist comfortable and let your elbow move naturally as you reach another string.
lessons.recap: You have extended your first-position map to the middle strings.

lessons.title: The bass strings
lessons.summary: A–B–C and low E–F–G.
lessons.see: String 5: A open, B at fret 2 with finger 2, C at fret 3 with finger 3. String 6: E open, F at fret 1 with finger 1, G at fret 3 with finger 3.
lessons.detail: Bass notes use ledger lines below the staff. Follow one line or space at a time rather than guessing from the distance. The board labels always show the sounding octave.
lessons.practice: Play the bass phrase at an easy tempo. Compare the low open E with the high open E from lesson 2. Keep the string order clear as you move between strings 6 and 5.
lessons.recap: You can locate natural notes across all six strings in first position.

lessons.title: Keep the pulse
lessons.summary: Count notes and silence.
lessons.see: In 4/4, count 1–2–3–4 evenly. A quarter note lasts one beat, a half note two beats, and two eighth notes divide one beat: say “1 and”. A rest is counted silence.
lessons.detail: The cursor keeps moving during a rest while the sounding marker disappears. Stop the string gently for a rest. BPM here counts quarter-note beats.
lessons.practice: Clap the rhythm first. Then play it on open E. Start slowly and count aloud. Try three loops, keeping the rests as steady as the notes.
lessons.recap: You can keep counting through long notes, short notes, and rests.

lessons.title: Your first melody
lessons.summary: Make a small musical sentence.
lessons.see: Use the notes you already know to play this original melody. Read a few notes ahead and prepare the next finger while the current note sounds.
lessons.detail: Practice the two bars separately, then join them. Long notes are a chance to breathe and prepare, not a reason to lose the beat.
lessons.practice: Choose a tempo where you can stay relaxed. Play one phrase, pause to reset, and play it again. Aim for a steady pulse rather than speed.
lessons.recap: You can combine note reading, string changes, and rhythm into a melody.

lessons.title: E minor
lessons.summary: Build your first open chord.
lessons.see: Place finger 2 on string 5 at fret 2 and finger 3 on string 4 at fret 2. Leave strings 6, 3, 2, and 1 open. Together these notes form E minor, written Em.
lessons.detail: A chord sounds several notes together. The board shows the whole shape. First check each string separately so you can hear whether every intended note rings.
lessons.practice: Choose String check and pick from string 6 to 1. Adjust any muffled note, then choose Chord to hear all six together. Strum gently downward and let it ring for four beats.
lessons.recap: You can build Em and check each of its six strings.

lessons.title: A minor
lessons.summary: Build Am and make a slow chord change.
lessons.see: For Am, place finger 1 on string 2 fret 1, finger 2 on string 4 fret 2, and finger 3 on string 3 fret 2. Play strings 5 through 1; leave string 6 out.
lessons.detail: An X means do not play that string. Check the five intended strings individually. Move slowly between Em and Am, letting the shape settle before the next strum.
lessons.practice: Practice the Am string check, then the Changes phrase. Strum on beat 1 and use the remaining beats to prepare. Pause between changes whenever you need to.
lessons.recap: You can form Am and move between two open chord shapes.

lessons.title: D major
lessons.summary: A smaller chord with a sharp.
lessons.see: Place finger 1 on string 3 fret 2, finger 3 on string 2 fret 3, and finger 2 on string 1 fret 2. Play from open string 4 down toward string 1. Omit strings 5 and 6.
lessons.detail: String 1 fret 2 is F-sharp: one fret above F. The sharp sign raises a note by one semitone. This F-sharp helps give D major its sound.
lessons.practice: Check the four strings separately. Keep fingertips curved enough for adjacent strings to ring, without forcing your hand. Then try one gentle four-string strum every four beats.
lessons.recap: You can read a sharp and form the open D-major shape.

lessons.title: Put it together
lessons.summary: Finish with melody and chord changes.
lessons.see: First play the melody using single notes. Then choose Chord changes for a separate Em–Am–D exercise. These are two activities: you do not need to play melody and chords at once.
lessons.detail: Review the notes or chord shapes whenever you need to. Progress means taking part and noticing what to practice next, not passing a speed test.
lessons.practice: Spend a minute on the melody and a minute changing chords slowly. Finish by choosing one earlier lesson to revisit. A few relaxed minutes repeated regularly are enough for a useful practice session.
lessons.recap: You have explored open strings, first-position notes, rhythm, a melody, and three chord shapes. Keep revisiting them at your own pace.

lessons.title: Control the eighth notes
lessons.summary: Keep a steady pick through string crossings.
lessons.see: Count 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and. A downstroke starts each numbered beat; an upstroke answers on “and”. Keep the motion small.
lessons.detail: The picking cue is separate from the fretting finger inside the marker. Start with open strings, then keep the same alternating motion while crossing between strings 2 and 1.
lessons.practice: Say the count before playing. Loop the first example until each pair is even, then play the crossing phrase. Choose a slower BPM whenever the upstroke catches.
lessons.recap: You can divide a beat evenly and carry alternate picking across a string change.

question.question: Which stroke follows a downstroke in this exercise?
question.hint: Keep alternating down and up, including across strings.

lessons.title: Play across the beat
lessons.summary: Hear the difference between a tie and a new attack.
lessons.see: A dotted quarter lasts one and a half beats. A tie joins two notes of the same pitch: hold through the second note instead of picking again.
lessons.detail: Keep counting during rests. In Across the barline, the open E crosses from beat 4 into the next measure. The sound continues, even though the notation needs two noteheads.
lessons.practice: Clap the dotted rhythm. Then count the rests and hold the tied E without another pick. Compare it with the repeated E near the end.
lessons.recap: You can separate silence, a held note, and a repeated attack.

question.question: What do you do at the second note of a tie?
question.hint: A tie holds the same pitch; it is not a new attack.

lessons.title: Feel six-eight
lessons.summary: Count two groups of three.
lessons.see: Say ONE two three FOUR five six. Each syllable is an eighth note; each group of three makes one dotted-quarter pulse.
lessons.detail: The BPM control still counts quarter notes. At 60 quarter-note BPM, the dotted-quarter pulse is 40 per minute. The six-eight grouping comes from your count, not a change to the slider’s unit.
lessons.practice: Clap two larger pulses while saying six subdivisions. Play the broken pattern with the same grouping, then let the dotted notes fill a complete group.
lessons.recap: You can read six-eight without treating it as six heavy beats.

question.question: How many eighth notes fill one dotted-quarter pulse?
question.hint: Count ONE two three as one larger pulse.

lessons.title: Move beyond first position
lessons.summary: Release, travel, and land with a guide finger.
lessons.see: Your index finger names the position. Let it guide you from fret 1 to fret 3 and then fret 5. Release pressing force before travelling; do not squeeze while moving.
lessons.detail: The position caption marks the intended hand location. Look at the landing fret before moving. A guide finger may lightly touch the string; this is a position shift, not a sounded slide.
lessons.practice: Step through each landing before using Play. Keep the thumb mobile and the wrist comfortable. Stop and reset if the hand feels forced.
lessons.recap: You can prepare a new position and land before picking.

question.question: What should happen before a position shift?
question.hint: Lighten the grip so the hand can move freely.

lessons.title: A minor pentatonic
lessons.summary: Map five notes across six strings.
lessons.see: The A-minor pentatonic scale contains A, C, D, E, and G. Start with index finger 1 at fret 5; use finger 3 at fret 7 and finger 4 at fret 8.
lessons.detail: Root rings mark A. Frets 5–8 form this position, even though the board also shows the nut for orientation. Say the note names instead of memorizing only a shape.
lessons.practice: Play the lower three strings first and then the upper three. Pause on every A. Use the second example to come back down without speeding up.
lessons.recap: You can find A roots and follow a fifth-position pentatonic route.

question.question: Which notes belong to A minor pentatonic?
question.hint: Use the five-note collection, with A as the home note.

lessons.title: Make a musical phrase
lessons.summary: Turn a scale into a question and answer.
lessons.see: A phrase has shape and space. Play a short idea, leave silence, then answer it. You do not have to use every note in the pattern.
lessons.detail: Listen for the A root as a resting place. The examples use the same pentatonic collection with different rhythms. Keep silences intentional and stop the string for each rest.
lessons.practice: Loop the call, then answer with the written response. Finally invent a two-note answer on the shown positions; the app is a reference, not a judge of your improvisation.
lessons.recap: You can use rhythm and silence to give a small group of notes a musical shape.

question.question: What can make a short phrase clearer?
answers: Playing every note as fast as possible
question.hint: A counted rest gives an idea room to breathe.

lessons.title: Fingerpicking foundations
lessons.summary: Let the thumb and fingers share the work.
lessons.see: Picking-hand letters are p for thumb, i for index, m for middle, and a for ring. They are not the fretting-hand numbers. Assign p to the bass and i–m–a to strings 3–2–1.
lessons.detail: Hold the Em or Am shape while the picking hand moves. Notes on different strings overlap and keep glowing until their written durations end. The blue marker shows the next attack, not a command to stop the others.
lessons.practice: Read each picking cue aloud. Keep the hand relaxed and pluck toward the palm with a small motion. First play one four-note cycle, then join two cycles.
lessons.recap: You can separate the roles of both hands and let a broken chord ring.

question.question: What does p mean in a picking cue?
question.hint: Letters describe the picking hand; numbers describe the fretting hand.

lessons.title: Small chords, clear voices
lessons.summary: Compare major and minor triads.
lessons.see: A triad contains a root, a third, and a fifth. These small shapes use only strings 3, 2, and 1. Leave the other strings out.
lessons.detail: Compare D major with D minor: only the highest note moves from F-sharp to F. Compare A major with A minor: the C-sharp on string 2 lowers to C. One semitone changes the chord quality.
lessons.practice: Check each shape one string at a time, then hear its three notes together. Keep the same pulse while changing and let your hand reset between attempts.
lessons.recap: You can hear and locate the note that changes a major triad into minor.

question.question: Which chord tone lowers to change major into minor?
question.hint: D major has F-sharp; D minor has F. This is its third.

lessons.title: Your first small barre
lessons.summary: One finger, two strings, without excess pressure.
lessons.see: Lay the side of index finger 1 across strings 1 and 2 at fret 1. Add finger 2 on string 3 fret 2. This small F shape uses only the top three strings.
lessons.detail: The bar on the diagram is one finger covering two strings. Bring it close behind the fret and use only enough pressure for clarity. Release between attempts; stop if anything hurts.
lessons.practice: Check strings 3, 2, and 1 individually. If one is muted, adjust the index angle instead of squeezing harder. Then alternate the shape with open E minor on the top strings.
lessons.recap: You can recognize a small barre and check both strings it covers.

question.question: What does the short barre represent?
answers: A capo across all six strings
question.hint: Index finger 1 covers strings 1 and 2 at fret 1.

lessons.title: Hammer-ons and ascending slurs
lessons.summary: Pick once, then sound the higher note.
lessons.see: Pick the lower note once, then bring the next fretting finger down clearly just behind its fret. The second note comes from the fretting hand. H and a curved slur connect the pair.
lessons.detail: A hammer-on changes pitch; a tie holds the same pitch. Keep the lower fretting finger placed for the fretted pair. Use a small controlled movement, not a large swing.
lessons.practice: Step through each pair to place the fingers. Use Play to hear the connected rhythm, then play it yourself with one initial pick. Keep both notes clear before increasing BPM.
lessons.recap: You can distinguish a hammer-on from a picked pair or a tie.

question.question: How many pick strokes begin a two-note hammer-on pair?
question.hint: Pick the first note; the fretting hand sounds the second.

lessons.title: Pull-offs and connected phrases
lessons.summary: Prepare the lower note before releasing the higher one.
lessons.see: Place the lower finger first. Pick the higher note, then make a small controlled plucking release with that fretting finger so the lower note sounds. P and a slur identify the pull-off.
lessons.detail: Simply lifting away may make the second note too quiet. Keep the prepared finger firm without excess force and avoid catching an unintended string. H rises in pitch; P falls.
lessons.practice: Practice descending pairs, then the three-note connected group. Pick only at the start of each group. Compare clarity at a slow tempo and take breaks.
lessons.recap: You can connect notes in both directions with prepared fingers.

question.question: What should be ready before a fretted pull-off?
answers: The lower finger is already placed
The lower finger stays in the air
question.hint: Prepare the destination before sounding the higher note.

lessons.title: Put the new skills together
lessons.summary: Two original studies, one step at a time.
lessons.see: Choose Lead study for position shifts, pentatonic phrases, and H/P connections. Choose Ringing triads for a separate fingerpicking study. You do not need to play both parts together.
lessons.detail: Practice two bars at a time. Before a shift, locate the landing fret; before a slur, prepare its destination. In fingerpicking, follow p–i–m–a while the fretting hand holds the shape.
lessons.practice: Play each study slowly, then revisit the bar that needed the most attention. Finish with one relaxed complete pass. Accuracy and comfort matter more than finishing at a particular speed.
lessons.recap: You have connected rhythm, fretboard movement, lead technique, and small chord textures. Choose your next practice focus and return whenever you like.

question.question: What is a useful response to a difficult bar?
answers: Slow down and isolate the transition
question.hint: Work on the small transition, then reconnect it to the phrase.
